title: How do trees affect the weather?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a tangent about Joyce Kilmer's poem "Trees" and the hosts' Atlanta forest surroundings, then cover global forest land and deforestation (about 13 million hectares lost per year, with a correction that a hectare is just over two acres). The main topic is how trees affect weather and climate in three ways: lowering temperatures through evapotranspiration (a large oak can transpire about 40 gallons a year), reducing energy use through deciduous shade and passive heating and cooling, and removing air pollutants, including the trade-off that tree volatile organic compounds contribute to photochemical smog. They discuss the urban heat island effect and albedo, carbon sequestration in forest soil, and carbon offset tree planting (Pearl Jam and Al Gore). They note that planting trees in the tropics cools the planet via clouds, while in boreal regions it can warm it, citing a 2013 Lawrence Livermore computer model on doubling forests. The episode closes with a listener mail from David Holbrook Jr. and a sponsor message.

segments.title: Opening banter and Joyce Kilmer
segments.summary: Hosts joke about misquoting Joyce Kilmer's tree poem and about living in the Atlanta forest, then introduce the idea that trees are both beautiful and functional.

segments.title: Global forest land and deforestation
segments.summary: Forest land is concentrated in about ten countries. Boreal, temperate, and rainforest zones are described. About 13 million hectares are lost each year to fires, disease, logging, and slash-and-burn. A hectare is just over two acres.

segments.title: Trees, climate, and the three ways they affect weather
segments.summary: Climate is defined as weather patterns over about thirty years. Global temperatures have risen one to one and a half degrees in the past century. Trees affect climate by lowering temperatures, reducing energy use, and removing pollutants.

segments.title: Evapotranspiration and natural air conditioning
segments.summary: Evaporation and transpiration release moisture that cools the air. A large oak can transpire about forty gallons of water a year.

segments.title: Passive heating and cooling with deciduous trees
segments.summary: Planting deciduous trees to the south and west shades homes in summer and lets sunlight through in winter, cutting energy costs. The hosts compare magnolias and pines as yard trees.

segments.title: Urban heat island effect and albedo
segments.summary: Dark surfaces like asphalt and roofs absorb heat, so cities run several degrees hotter than suburbs. Atlanta and Phoenix are cited as examples. Trees help counteract this.

segments.title: Air pollution removal and tree VOCs causing smog
segments.summary: Trees filter dust, ozone, carbon monoxide, and other pollutants, and absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis. Trees also release volatile organic compounds that speed the formation of ozone and photochemical smog. Ronald Reagan's claim that trees pollute more than cars is mentioned.

segments.title: Carbon offsets, Pearl Jam, and where to plant trees
segments.summary: Pearl Jam and Al Gore offset tour emissions by planting trees. Tropical trees cool the planet via clouds, while trees in boreal regions can warm it by lowering albedo. A 2013 Lawrence Livermore model suggests doubling forests could lower global temperature by a degree Fahrenheit.

segments.title: Sponsor message
segments.summary: Brief message break mentioned and a sponsor read for BASF at the end of the episode.

segments.title: Listener mail from David Holbrook Jr.
segments.summary: A listener from Mississippi shares his praise for the show, his jobs, and his regional accent, and mentions his family's chicken farm. The hosts sign off with calls for feedback.
